title: Using artificial windows to influence occupants' mood and task performance in windowless spaces - A review
review_question: This paper analyzes benefits of windows, summarizes prior studies on artificial windows' impact on occupants' mood and work productivity, scrutinizes experimental design and evaluation methods, reflects the limitations of previous studies on artificial windows experiments, and proposes potential improvements for future research.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: The review focuses on research articles examining the effects of artificial windows on occupants' psychological emotions and work efficiency, experimental design, and assessment methods. It includes studies on both artificial side-window and skylight systems, and their impact on mood, stress, well-being, and task performance.

synthesis_conclusions: Subjects tend to experience higher positive emotions and less stress when exposed to artificial windows.
Artificial windows may connect occupants in confined spaces with the outdoors, compared to spaces without windows.
There is a lack of research evidence regarding the improvement in task performance from artificial windows.
Artificial windows may serve as viable substitutes in windowless environments due to progress in simulating daylight and window views.

Research on artificial windows is relatively limited, primarily focusing on temporary effects in office environments, with insufficient attention to real-scene applications, long-term evaluation, and diverse user groups.
A combination of multiple evaluation methods (subjective, physiological, task performance) is suggested for comprehensive assessment of artificial windows' effects.
New assessment techniques like facial expression recognition and eye movement analysis should be explored in future research.
evidence_gaps: Lack of research evidence regarding the improvement in objective task performance from artificial windows.
Insufficient exploration of dynamic real-time simulation of the outdoor environment by artificial windows and comparison of perceived realism between artificial and real windows.
Research on artificial windows is relatively limited, primarily focusing on temporary effects in office environments.
Insufficient attention to the application effects of artificial windows in various real scenes and their long-term evaluation on human physical and mental health.
The influence between different application scenarios of artificial windows and their diverse users has not been fully explored.
Most previous artificial window studies have been conducted in laboratory settings, limiting generalizability to real-life behavioral and psychophysiological states.
Need for research exploring psychological and physiological impacts on occupants in various types of spaces (e.g., classrooms, hospital wards, underground spaces).
Need for studies under real field conditions to comprehensively and accurately assess subjects' performance with artificial windows.
The existing research population in human skylight studies is mostly concentrated in middle-aged and young stages, neglecting children, the elderly, and different occupations.
Most current studies on artificial skylights are short-term; long-term experiment research is urgently needed.
Subjective assessment methods have validity concerns; a combination of subjective and objective evidence is needed.
Physiological indicators are susceptible to various environmental and human-induced interferences, requiring more robust assessment methods.
limitations: Most studies are short-term and conducted in laboratory settings, limiting generalizability to real-life, long-term scenarios and diverse functional environments.
The research population is often limited to young/middle-aged adults, neglecting children, the elderly, and different occupations who may have distinct responses.
Subjective assessment methods, while common, have validity concerns and may not fully reflect real thoughts/feelings.
Objective measures (physiological, task performance) are susceptible to environmental and human interferences, and require more sophisticated multi-method approaches.
There is insufficient exploration of dynamic real-time simulation and perceived realism of artificial windows compared to real windows.
A lack of consistent evidence regarding the improvement in objective task performance.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Artificial windows displaying natural content can provide restorative experiences similar to real nature, thereby improving directed attention and reducing mental fatigue.

Humans have an innate tendency to connect with nature, and artificial windows simulating natural views can partially satisfy this biophilic need, leading to positive psychological and physiological outcomes.

mechanism_chain.description: Artificial windows, particularly those with dynamic and natural content, enhance perceived naturalness and realism, which in turn triggers restorative processes and positive affective responses, leading to improved mood and cognitive performance.
